To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) in diabetic RBC, glucose and lactate contents are higher, and ATP levels similar to normal RBCs; (2) in diabetic R BCs incubated in diabetic plasma, glucose levels decrease and lactate increase, but ATP levels remain unchanged; and (3) in diabetic R B C s incubated in normal plasmas, ATP levels decrease, but glucose and lactate levels are similar to controls.
in non-insulin dependent diabetic subjects, the erythrocyte ATP concentration is lower than normal, and this is associated with increased lactate and decreased glucose levels.

the metabolic behaviour of erythrocytes from diabetic subjects incubated in their own plasma is different from that of normal subjects, but becomes similar when incubated in plasma from normal individuals.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of RBC metabolism and the role of plasma as a modulating factor in diabetic subjects.
the metabolic behaviour of RBCs in the presence of their own plasma and normal plasma in diabetic patients.
the metabolic behaviour of erythrocytes incubated over a period of time in their own plasma or in isologous plasma.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
in diabetes the erythrocyte is not an inert cell, but a dynamic and functional cell that can be influenced by the metabolic state of the organism.
RBCs from diabetic patients are characterized by an increased lactate and glucose content, but a normal ATP content; these metabolic changes are probably related to a defect in RBC glycolytic flux.
the metabolic behaviour of RBCs in diabetic patients, as well as in healthy subjects, depends on the metabolic status of the plasma in which RBCs are incubated.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
in diabetic RBC, glucose is increased, ATP is decreased and glycolysis is increased.

the metabolic behaviour of diabetic RBCs incubated in normal or diabetic plasma is not the result of the presence of a specific metabolic defect in the erythrocytes, but is due to the different metabolic behaviour of the plasma in the two groups.

the diabetic erythrocyte, when incubated in its own plasma, is unable to decrease its intracellular glucose content, and therefore it cannot produce ATP, and the excess glucose is converted into lactate.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the RBCs from diabetic patients are able to respond to the normal plasma environment, which suggests that the RBC membrane has the potential to adapt to a new environment.
erythrocytes can be considered as a good model for the study of metabolic disorders in diabetic subjects.
erythrocytes from non-insulin dependent diabetic subjects are able to metabolize glucose and lactate in a different way from those of control subjects.
